title: New to RPG Maker – Which version should I get (MV or MZ) for a game like Leyley or Fear & Hunger?

posts.author: Marsierra
posts.body:
Hey everyone!
I know this question has been asked a lot, sorry! But which RPG Maker version is best for a game like
The Coffin of Andy and Leyley and
Fear and Hunger.
Lately, I’ve been thinking about getting into game development, but I’m still researching which engine to use. I haven’t really come across any solid tutorials for RPG Maker so far. So I feel a bit scared to approach the engine.
I want to create something similar to
The Coffin of Andy and Leyley, Fear and Hunger or To the Moon
. I know these games were made using RPG Maker, and I really love their atmosphere and design style — that’s what inspired me to try making something similar myself.
I was also wondering: with RPG Maker, do I have the freedom to use my
own custom art and pixel assets
instead of the built-in ones?
I’m completely new to all of this, so I apologize if my questions sound a bit silly. I’m just really eager to learn and would appreciate any advice or tutorial recommendations you can share.
Also, for a game like the ones I mentioned, should I get
RPG Maker MV
or
RPG Maker MZ
?

posts.author: TotalyNate
posts.body:
I would suggest mz because I feel like the plugin library is larger. There are built In tutorials as well as tutorials by cazwolf, level up design, and others on YouTube. And creating your own art and music for mz is easy.
If the yanfly plugins were still free, I would recommend mv probably, as I personally prefer the rtp from mv. But yeah mz is the right choice.

posts.author: Piyan Glupak
posts.body:
I have used MV to make a couple of games, but am doing my current project in MZ. Both are good, capable versions of RPG Maker. I was surprised at how many MV plugins work with MZ. Many of the ones that don't seem to be scene related.
MV needs plugins for a few things that come as standard with MZ but not MV. For instance, I like the forest auto-tiles  on the overworld sheet A2 to have '*' passability. (I have a plugin that does that for MV, but you can do that in the editor for MZ.) You need a plugin that lets MV cope with certain monitors. On the other hand, there seem to be a wider range of plugins available. I have used a plugin that makes the battle user interface work well for a battle party of 6; so far I haven't had anything work for me in MZ. As stated above, MV plugins are usually free, or likely to be cheaper than MZ ones. MV is stable; I like this because you don't need to worry about what future updates will affect.
MV can deploy for Linux, but I understand that only older Mac's are catered for, wheras MZ can't deploy for Linux, but can for current Mac systems.
MZ has "quality of life" features that MV doesn't. I suspect that Avery takes more advantage of the better mapping than I do, but I find it very useful at times. Some of the new features don't interest me, for instance, I have to remember to turn-off autosave whenever I start a new project. The movement route indicator is useful when an event moves itself, but not worth it when it moves another event or the party. On plugins written for MZ (some of which work on MV), there seems to be some very good ones with wonderful player interfaces, but the plugins can be a lot bigger than the equivalent MV ones. I get the impression that the plugin gap between MV and MZ is closing.
I am quite sure that you are capable of downloading the trial versions of both MV and MZ. The main factor in which one you choose might depend upon what plugins are available to achieve the game you want. I can't give advice on that without more detailed questions because I am not familiar with the games you mentioned.

The cookie cutter molds are a double edged sword that is both RPG Maker's strength and weakness. People that do pick RPG Maker do it partly BECAUSE of the templates, i.e. a lot of work is already done for you. The downside is now "All RPG Maker games look/play/feel the same", you need plugins to break away from the templates, an increasing number of which are paywalled. In addition, the more you want to change things, the more work it is, and the less reason there is to use RPG Maker over another engine, where you have complete control of everything from the beginning because you built it.
What does a Godot game look like? Game Maker? Construct? Etc. Those engines are less reliant on templates so don't have a distinct look and are far more flexible in the games they can make.

posts.body:
Marsierra said:
Also, for a game like the ones I mentioned, should I get

RPG Maker MZ

Click to expand...
Ultimately, MV and MZ are
more or less
the same engine. At this point, I would say the only reasons to choose MV over MZ are niche reasons such as:
You started your game in MV (probably before MZ was released) and don't want the trouble of porting it to the newer engine. (For the record: This is my reason for using MV.)
You absolutely need a plugin that's only available for MV and you can't find an MZ equivalent that'll work, especially if the plugin doesn't work well with FOSSIL.
Your budget is tight and you feel that paying the (presumably) higher price for MZ would be pushing your luck.
Again: at a fundamental level, the differences between MV and MZ are very minimal. Pretty much anything you can do in MV can also be done in MZ and vice versa. Some things are easier to do in MZ though – for example, if you want an ATB battle system, then MZ gives you that (at least the basics of it) out of the box. (But there are tons of ATB plugins for MV as well, so it's not like you
have
to use MZ to have ATB.)
In short: unless you have a very, very compelling reason to choose MV? Don't. Use MZ instead.

Have you used a general purpose engine before? The difference between the power and flexibility of Godot, GameMaker, Construct etc and RPG Maker is that they are more open ended with fewer pre-built systems and freedom to design everything exactly how you want. Thus you can't define what a Godot or Construct game looks like the same way you can with RPG Maker. RPG Maker gives you a bunch of pre-built templates. Many of the thousands of RPG Maker plugins are just overwriting bits of template engine code so you can tweak one small aspect of one of the templates.
If you specifically want RPG templates and prebuilt systems, RPG Maker has direct free competitors like EasyRPG and Wolf RPG, and even more paid ones like Architect, Bakin, RPG in a Box, etc.

I'd have to research it to give you the full details, but in essence, an RPGMaker game is literally just a website and minimal browser (specifically nwjs) bundled together. Take a Windows-deployed game, delete the Windows version of the browser, and put in a Linux version of the browser… and you have a Linux version of your game. (Or take the web-deployed game and drop in the browser.)
AquaEcho said:
The difference between the power and flexibility of Godot, GameMaker, Construct etc and RPG Maker is that they are more open ended with fewer pre-built systems and freedom to design everything exactly how you want.
Click to expand...
This is a double-edged sword. Yes, you can make it exactly how you want, certainly… but it's not necessarily
easier
to make it that way. If "exactly how you want" happens to be pretty close to RPGMaker default, it really is better to just use RPGMaker instead of Godot. Naturally, that applies equally for the others you mentioned (EasyRPG, RPG in a Box etc). Of course, if "exactly how you want" is pretty far from RPGMaker, then you probably have a point that a generic engine like Godot or Unreal would be better than RPGMaker.

Actually, I didn’t want to open this can of worms, but maybe it is productive if I, as a plugin developer, give some additional insights. Yes, as I already said, I constantly get requests to make my plugins compatible with VS or others, and believe me, those requests are even more annoying than normal bug reports.
But I can tell you this: so far, I’ve always been able to solve it somehow. I’m used to black-boxing anyway, and code isn’t the only thing we developers have. For example, all of VS’s monkey patches are publicly visible with the debugger and therefore also switchable, and apparently many devs don’t know that.
Here’s an example where the plugin developer was in the wrong. I recently came across a plugin whose developer rejected such a request with the justification “can’t see the code, not doing it.” And sorry to put it this way, but that was complete nonsense. An experienced programmer could have solved that easily. The developer was either too inexperienced or too lazy. I checked his code out of curiosity and, well… it was almost a miracle that his plugin worked at all.
Does that mean I always defend VS? (After all, I respect Yanfly and Yanfly also respects me) But no, there are also things VS doesn’t handle correctly in my opinion. For example, Blizzard’s UltraMode7 stopped working and could only be fixed after he rolled back certain parts of the VS code. Also, in my opinion, when you touch rmmz_core, you...
- must be fully transparent
- must add plugin parameters to individually switch off every modification
- must not add any plugin that requires "VS Core" to work
This is actually something that I criticize about VS and starts myself to slowly stop using their plugins.
In the end, the answer is somewhere in the middle. There are conflicts that can’t be solved without code insight or their help, but they’re far fewer than people make them out to be. The hate is not justified in my opinion.

posts.author: Echowake
posts.body:
AquaEcho said:
The cookie cutter molds are a double edged sword that is both RPG Maker's strength and weakness. People that do pick RPG Maker do it partly BECAUSE of the templates, i.e. a lot of work is already done for you. The downside is now "All RPG Maker games look/play/feel the same", you need plugins to break away from the templates, an increasing number of which are paywalled. In addition, the more you want to change things, the more work it is, and the less reason there is to use RPG Maker over another engine, where you have complete control of everything from the beginning because you built it.
What does a Godot game look like? Game Maker? Construct? Etc. Those engines are less reliant on templates so don't have a distinct look and are far more flexible in the games they can make.
